title: Explain the Spark master-worker architecture — Driver (SparkSession/SparkContext, DAG, task scheduling), Cluster Manager (Standalone/YARN/K8s/Databricks), Worker Nodes, Executors (JVM processes on workers), and Tasks (smallest unit, one per partition).
shortTitle: Spark master-worker architecture — Driver, Cluster Manager, Workers, Executors, Tasks

s1_definition.profdef: Spark uses a master-worker (driver-executor) architecture. The Driver is the master process that hosts the SparkSession, builds the logical and physical plan as a DAG, and schedules work. The Cluster Manager (Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or a managed service like Databricks) allocates compute resources across the cluster. Worker Nodes are the physical or virtual machines that provide those resources, and on them the Cluster Manager launches Executors, which are long-lived JVM processes that actually run the work and hold cached data. The smallest unit of work is a Task, and Spark creates one Task per partition per stage, running many Tasks in parallel across Executors.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India processing year-end statements for millions of accounts. The Driver is the branch manager who holds the master plan and decides who does what. The Cluster Manager is the HR department that assigns desks and staff. The Worker Nodes are the office floors with desks. The Executors are the clerks sitting at those desks who actually do the counting and keep their working papers in front of them. A Task is one clerk processing one box of account files. If there are two hundred boxes, the manager splits the job into two hundred tasks and hands them to the clerks, who work in parallel.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Driver plans and schedules, the Cluster Manager allocates resources, Executors run Tasks in parallel on Worker Nodes, and one Task processes one partition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark uses a master-worker (driver-executor) architecture. The Driver is the master process that hosts the SparkSession, builds the logical and physical plan as a DAG, and schedules work. The Cluster Manager (Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or a managed service like Databricks) allocates compute resources across the cluster. Worker Nodes are the physical or virtual machines that provide those resources, and on them the Cluster Manager launches Executors, which are long-lived JVM processes that actually run the work and hold cached data. The smallest unit of work is a Task, and Spark creates one Task per partition per stage, running many Tasks in parallel across Executors.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India processing year-end statements for millions of accounts. The Driver is the branch manager who holds the master plan and decides who does what. The Cluster Manager is the HR department that assigns desks and staff. The Worker Nodes are the office floors with desks. The Executors are the clerks sitting at those desks who actually do the counting and keep their working papers in front of them. A Task is one clerk processing one box of account files. If there are two hundred boxes, the manager splits the job into two hundred tasks and hands them to the clerks, who work in parallel.

**One line to remember:** The Driver plans and schedules, the Cluster Manager allocates resources, Executors run Tasks in parallel on Worker Nodes, and one Task processes one partition.

sections.s2_technical:
The Driver is the heart of a Spark application. When you create a SparkSession (which wraps the older SparkContext), you start the Driver process. The Driver is where your main program runs, where transformations are recorded into a logical plan, where the DAG (directed acyclic graph) of stages is built, and where the two schedulers live. The DAGScheduler breaks the job into stages at shuffle boundaries, and the TaskScheduler sends individual tasks to executors and tracks their completion. The Driver also holds the metadata about the application and collects final results when an action like collect runs. If the Driver dies, the whole application dies, which is why in production you run it in cluster mode on a stable node.

The Cluster Manager is pluggable. Spark does not insist on one resource manager; it works with its own Standalone manager, with Hadoop YARN, with Kubernetes, or with a managed platform like Databricks. The Cluster Manager's job is narrow but essential: when the Driver requests executors with a certain number of cores and amount of memory, the Cluster Manager finds room on the worker nodes and launches those executor processes. For example, requesting five executors each with four cores and eight gigabytes of memory is a request the Cluster Manager satisfies by placing JVM processes across the available machines.

Worker Nodes are simply the machines in the cluster that contribute CPU and memory. Executors are the JVM processes launched on those worker nodes, and they are long-lived for the duration of the application. Each executor has a fixed number of cores and a memory allocation, runs multiple tasks concurrently (one task per core), and keeps cached RDD or DataFrame partitions in its memory so later stages can reuse them without recomputation. Executors also report their status back to the Driver with heartbeats.

A Task is the smallest unit of execution, and the key rule to remember is one task per partition per stage. If a DataFrame has two hundred partitions and the current stage runs a map-like operation, Spark creates two hundred tasks for that stage, and they are distributed across the executor cores. The degree of parallelism you actually get is the minimum of the number of partitions and the total number of executor cores. A senior nuance is that too few partitions underutilize the cluster while too many create scheduling overhead, so tuning partition count against total cores is one of the most practical performance levers. In a banking job this is the difference between finishing the nightly settlement reconciliation in twenty minutes versus two hours.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank must process millions of transactions for a nightly report, and no single machine is big enough. This is exactly why Spark splits the data into partitions and spreads tasks across many executors.

Problem 2 — Someone must hold the master plan and decide how to break the job into stages and tasks. This is exactly the role of the Driver and its schedulers.

Problem 3 — Someone must provide and launch the worker processes. This is exactly the Cluster Manager allocating resources and starting Executors on Worker Nodes.

Because a real cluster is heavy, the mini-project simulates the architecture in Java. `Driver` holds the plan and splits a transaction dataset into partitions, builds tasks (one per partition), and submits them. `ClusterManager` launches a set of `Executor` worker threads. Each `Executor` runs `Task` objects in parallel, each task summing one partition of Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, and the Driver collects the partial results into a final total. This mirrors driver planning, cluster-manager allocation, executor parallelism, and one-task-per-partition.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the architecture simulation
java -cp target/spark-architecture-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.sparkarch.SparkArchDemo

# For reference, how the REAL job is submitted to a cluster:
spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 5 \
  --executor-cores 4 \
  --executor-memory 8g \
  --class com.bank.sparkarch.NightlyReportJob \
  nightly-report.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: twenty transactions — ten of Rs.1000 for Rajesh (SAV2001) and ten of Rs.500 for Priya (CUR3001), totalling Rs.15000. The Cluster Manager grants four cores; the Driver requests eight partitions.

Step 1: The Driver builds the plan. It decides to split the twenty transactions into eight partitions, which means it will create eight tasks. The data is still in the Driver's list at this point.

Step 2: The Driver partitions the data round-robin, so each of the eight partitions holds two or three transactions. Nothing is computed yet; the partitions are just lists.

Step 3: The Driver creates one Task per partition — eight Task objects — each owning exactly one partition. This is the one-task-per-partition rule in action.

Step 4: The Driver submits the eight tasks to the Cluster Manager. The Cluster Manager has four cores, so it launches four Executors and runs the eight tasks in two waves of four, in parallel.

Step 5: Each Executor runs its Task's compute method, which sums the amounts in its single partition. The partial results stay on the executors momentarily and are returned to the Driver as each future completes.

Step 6: The Driver aggregates the eight partial sums into one final total of Rs.15000 and logs it as the nightly report result. The data has moved from one Driver list, to eight partitions, to eight parallel partial sums, back to one total.

```text

    │
    ▼
  DRIVER (master process, holds SparkSession + DAG + schedulers)
    │ partition(data, 8)  → 8 partitions
    │ create 1 Task per partition → Task0..Task7
    ▼
  CLUSTER MANAGER (YARN/K8s/Standalone) — grants 4 cores
    │ launches Executors, schedules 8 tasks over 4 cores (2 waves)
    ├────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
    ▼            ▼            ▼            ▼
  Executor-0   Executor-1   Executor-2   Executor-3
  Task0 sum    Task1 sum    Task2 sum    Task3 sum   ... then Task4..7
    │            │            │            │
    └────────────┴─────┬──────┴────────────┘
                       │ partial sums returned
                       ▼
  DRIVER aggregates partials → FINAL TOTAL = Rs.15000
                       │
                       ▼
  Output: "Nightly report total transaction amount = Rs.15000"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark uses a master-worker architecture built around five roles. The Driver is the master process; it hosts the SparkSession, runs my main program, records transformations into a DAG, and contains the DAGScheduler, which breaks the job into stages at shuffle boundaries, and the TaskScheduler, which dispatches individual tasks. The Cluster Manager — which can be Spark Standalone, Hadoop YARN, Kubernetes, or a managed platform like Databricks — is responsible only for allocating resources; when the Driver asks for executors with a certain number of cores and amount of memory, the Cluster Manager finds room on the worker nodes and launches those processes.

The Worker Nodes are the machines that contribute CPU and memory, and on them the Cluster Manager starts Executors, which are long-lived JVM processes. Each executor runs multiple tasks concurrently, one per core, and holds cached partitions in its memory so later stages can reuse them. The smallest unit of work is a Task, and the rule I always keep in mind is one task per partition per stage: if a stage runs over two hundred partitions, Spark creates two hundred tasks and spreads them across the executor cores. The real parallelism I get is the minimum of the partition count and the total number of executor cores.

In my project at the National Bank of India this architecture ran our nightly reconciliation and reporting jobs. The Driver planned the job and split the transaction data into partitions, YARN allocated five executors with four cores and eight gigabytes each, and the executors processed partitions in parallel while the Driver aggregated the results. The practical lesson I learned is that partition count is one of the biggest performance levers — too few partitions leave cores idle, too many create scheduling overhead — so I tuned the number of partitions against the total executor cores to keep the whole cluster busy and finish the nightly job inside its window.
